questions.question: What two topics does chapter 20 cover?
questions.answer: Important takeaways from the book, and resources for learning further and applying your skills in practice.
questions.explanation: Listed in the 'This chapter covers' box.

questions.question: What is section 20.1 intended for?
options: Introducing new architectures not covered earlier
A brief synthesis of key takeaways usable as a quick refresher
questions.answer: A brief synthesis of key takeaways usable as a quick refresher
questions.explanation: The page says 20.1 briefly synthesizes key takeaways and can be read as a quick refresher. It doesn't introduce new material; Kaggle appears in 20.4; the AGI remark was on p.618.

questions.question: Which sections of chapter 20 address staying up to date, and what resources do they name?
questions.answer: Section 20.4: practicing on real-world problems with Kaggle, reading new developments on arXiv, and exploring the Keras ecosystem.
questions.explanation: From the chapter outline (pp.631-632).

questions.question: Why do the authors describe finishing the book as 'merely your first step'?
questions.answer: Because becoming an effective AI practitioner requires continued practice and learning in a fast-moving field; the book provides foundations and the chapter aims to equip you to continue on your own.
questions.explanation: Paraphrases the second intro paragraph and motivates 20.4.

questions.question: Before reading 20.1, list from memory the five or six ideas you consider most important in the book. Compare with the review afterward.
questions.answer: Answers vary.
questions.explanation: Active recall before reading a summary strengthens retention and reveals gaps to revisit.

questions.question: Which statement about the relationship between the fields is correct according to this page?
options: Generative AI is a subset of deep learning, which is a branch of machine learning, which is a subfield of AI.
Machine learning is a subset of deep learning.
AI and machine learning are synonyms; deep learning is separate.
Generative AI is a separate field alongside deep learning within machine learning.
questions.answer: Generative AI is a subset of deep learning, which is a branch of machine learning, which is a subfield of AI.
questions.explanation: The four bullets define exactly this nesting. ML contains DL (not the reverse); AI is broader than ML (it includes non-learning systems such as spreadsheets); and the page explicitly calls generative AI 'a specific subset of deep learning'.

questions.question: Why does the page emphasize that the chain of geometric transformations is differentiable?
questions.answer: Because differentiability is what allows the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight to be computed (via backpropagation), so the weights can be updated efficiently by gradient descent.
questions.explanation: Without derivatives you would have no direction in which to move the weights other than by costly trial and error. The page ties efficient weight updates directly to differentiability.

questions.question: What does it mean that generative models are trained in a 'self-supervised' manner? Give the two examples the page uses.
questions.answer: Their targets are derived from the input itself: they learn to reconstruct artificially missing or corrupted parts of the input. Examples: denoising images and predicting the next word in a sentence.
questions.explanation: Self-supervision removes the need for human labels, which lets these models train on very large datasets.

questions.question: According to the page, where is a deep learning model's knowledge stored, and what does learning consist of?
questions.answer: In its weights; learning consists of finding good values for the weights, values that minimize a loss function.
questions.explanation: This is stated verbatim in the deep learning bullet and matches the framework of p.32.

questions.question: Why does the page call an Excel spreadsheet an example of AI?
options: Because AI is defined broadly as all attempts to automate human cognitive processes, learning or not.
Because spreadsheets contain machine learning models.
Because spreadsheets are trained on data.
questions.answer: Because AI is defined broadly as all attempts to automate human cognitive processes, learning or not.
questions.explanation: The definition is about automating cognition, not about learning. Spreadsheets do not learn from data and are not ML models; differentiability is irrelevant to the definition of AI.

questions.question: The page says deep learning layers form 'stacks of layers—or, more generally, graphs of layers'. Give an example from the book of a model that is a graph rather than a stack.
questions.answer: Any model with a residual connection (e.g. the ResNet/Xception-style models of chapter 9) or a multi-input/multi-output model built with the Functional API (chapter 7).
questions.explanation: In such models some layer outputs feed into more than one later layer, or inputs merge, so the topology is a directed acyclic graph rather than a single chain.

questions.question: Without looking, explain to a friend in four sentences the difference between AI, ML, deep learning, and generative AI. Then compare with the four bullets on this page.
questions.answer: Your explanation should mention: automating cognition (AI); learning programs from data (ML); differentiable chains of layers trained by gradient descent (DL); large self-supervised models that generate content (generative AI).
questions.explanation: Recalling definitions without the text is the best check that you have internalized them.

questions.question: What, according to the page, distinguishes the current AI summer from previous ones?
options: Deep learning has provided enormous business value and become a huge consumer success.
It is driven by hand-coded expert systems.
It has achieved general human-level intelligence.
questions.answer: Deep learning has provided enormous business value and become a huge consumer success.
questions.explanation: The page says 'in stark contrast with previous AI summers' deep learning has delivered business value and consumer success. It explicitly says the end of the period is debated (so not 'never end'), expert systems belonged to an earlier boom, and the book nowhere claims general intelligence has been achieved.

questions.question: Complete the page's recipe: 'all you need is sufficiently large ___ trained with ___ on sufficiently many ___.'
questions.answer: parametric models; gradient descent; examples
questions.explanation: This sentence captures the 'surprising simplicity' of deep learning.

questions.question: Explain in geometric terms what a deep learning model does to an input, using the vocabulary of the page.
questions.answer: The input is vectorized into a point in an input space. Each layer applies a simple geometric transformation; the chain of layers forms a complex transformation that maps the point into the target space, ideally close to its target. The transformation's weights are updated iteratively based on how well the model performs.
questions.explanation: This restates the 'everything is a vector' paragraph; it is the mental model introduced on p.62.

questions.question: Why are the authors optimistic about deep learning even if research progress stopped?
questions.answer: Because deploying existing algorithms to every applicable problem would by itself be a game changer for most industries.
questions.explanation: The argument separates new capabilities from diffusion of existing ones; the latter alone justifies the optimism and will take decades.

questions.question: In 'This complex transformation attempts to map the input space to the target space, one point at a time,' what is 'one point'?
options: A single vectorized sample (e.g., one image or one sentence)
A single weight of the model
questions.answer: A single vectorized sample (e.g., one image or one sentence)
questions.explanation: Since everything is a vector, each sample is a point in the input space. Weights parameterize the transformation, layers are its steps, and epochs are passes over the data, none of which are 'points' being mapped.

questions.question: Pick a dataset from the book (e.g., IMDb reviews or MNIST). Can you describe its input vector space and its target vector space?
questions.answer: Example: MNIST inputs are 784-dimensional vectors (28×28 pixels, rescaled to [0,1]); targets are integers 0-9 (or 10-dimensional one-hot vectors), with model outputs in a 10-dimensional probability space.
questions.explanation: Being able to name both spaces is the practical meaning of 'everything is a vector'.

questions.question: In the paper-ball metaphor, what corresponds to a single layer of the model?
options: One movement of the person's hands on the paper ball
The full sequence of uncrumpling gestures
questions.answer: One movement of the person's hands on the paper ball
questions.explanation: The page maps each movement to one layer's simple transformation. The ball is the input data manifold, the full gesture sequence is the whole model, and the sheet colors (from chapter 2's version) represent classes.

questions.question: What are the two core ideas on which geometric meaning representations hinge?
questions.answer: That meaning is derived from the pairwise relationships between things, and that these relationships can be captured by a distance function.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in italics on the page.

questions.question: Why is differentiability called 'a significant constraint' rather than a mere technicality?
questions.answer: Because it forces the input-to-output mapping to be smooth and continuous: nearby inputs must map to nearby outputs, so the model can only approximate abrupt, discrete, or rule-like behavior. This shapes what can be learned and how the model generalizes.
questions.explanation: Gradient descent needs derivatives; the price is restricting the class of representable functions to smooth ones.

questions.question: Which of these does the page NOT propose as a better name for neural networks?
questions.answer: Artificial brains
questions.explanation: The other three are listed on the page (along with hierarchical representations learning). The page explicitly says neural networks have hardly anything to do with the brain, so 'artificial brains' contradicts its point.

questions.question: Name the two enabling factors listed on this page and the specific algorithmic milestone of 2017.
questions.answer: Incremental algorithmic innovations (starting with backpropagation) and the availability of large amounts of image, video, and text data; the 2017 milestone is the Transformer architecture.
questions.explanation: Hardware (GPUs) and software (CUDA, frameworks, Keras) follow on p.623.

questions.question: The page says all you need are 'spaces of sufficiently high dimensionality'. What could go wrong if an intermediate representation is too low-dimensional?
questions.answer: It cannot hold all the relevant relationships at once, so information is lost (an information bottleneck), and the model cannot separate what it needs to separate.
questions.explanation: Chapter 4's Reuters example showed accuracy dropping when a 4-unit intermediate layer was used for 46 classes.

questions.question: Draw the paper-ball picture for a two-class problem and annotate it with: input manifold, layer, model, and the moment the classes become linearly separable.
questions.answer: Your sketch should show a crumpled ball (input manifold), a few intermediate stages (each a layer), and a final flat configuration where a straight line separates the two colors (output of the model, fed to the final classifier).
questions.explanation: Producing the picture yourself checks that you can map each metaphor element to a model component.

questions.question: For a temporal prediction problem, how should validation and test data relate to training data?
options: They should be posterior to (come after) the training data.
They should be randomly sampled from the same time period as training data.
They should precede the training data.
They should overlap with the training data to ensure similar distributions.
questions.answer: They should be posterior to (come after) the training data.
questions.explanation: The page states this explicitly. Random sampling or earlier data lets the model exploit information from the 'future' relative to what it predicts, and overlap is a direct leak.

questions.question: List the three components of the software stack named on the page (with examples).
questions.answer: The CUDA language; frameworks that do automatic differentiation (TensorFlow, JAX, PyTorch); and Keras, which makes deep learning accessible to most people.
questions.explanation: These are the items of the fourth enabling factor.

questions.question: Why does the page say that tools like Keras and TensorFlow cannot help with the hardest part of the workflow?
questions.answer: Because deciding what to predict, from which data, and how to measure success requires understanding the problem domain; these are framing decisions outside the scope of any modeling library.
questions.explanation: Frameworks automate model building and training, not problem definition or metric choice.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the workflow steps listed on this page?
options: Deploy your final model in production
Identify a way to reliably measure success
questions.answer: Deploy your final model in production
questions.explanation: Deployment is a later step, listed on p.624. The other three are steps 1, 2, and 4 on this page.

questions.question: Give an example where plain accuracy would be a poor 'measure of success' and suggest a better one.
questions.answer: Fraud detection where 99.9% of transactions are legitimate: a model that predicts 'not fraud' always has 99.9% accuracy but is useless. Precision/recall, ROC AUC, or a cost-weighted metric are better.
questions.explanation: The page notes that beyond simple tasks success often requires sophisticated, domain-specific metrics.

questions.question: What hardware enabling factor does the page highlight, and what bet does it mention?
questions.answer: Fast, highly parallel, low-cost hardware, especially NVIDIA GPUs (gaming GPUs, then purpose-built chips); NVIDIA's CEO Jensen Huang bet the company's future on deep learning, which paid off.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first full bullet of the page.

questions.question: Think of a prediction problem from your own work. Can you answer steps 1-3 for it: the target, the available data, the success metric, and a leak-free split?
questions.answer: A complete answer names the target variable, the data source and labeling needs, a metric aligned with the real goal, and a split strategy (chronological if time matters).
questions.explanation: Practicing the framing steps on your own problem is the best preparation for real projects.

questions.question: According to the page, which data should guide changes to your model during refinement?
options: A combination of training and test data
questions.answer: Validation data only
questions.explanation: The page says: 'Make changes based on performance on the validation data only, not the test data or the training data.' Training performance rewards memorization, and using the test set for decisions removes your unbiased final estimate.

questions.question: Why should you first get your model to overfit before adding regularization?
questions.answer: Overfitting shows the model has a capacity level greater than needed; once you know capacity is not the bottleneck, you can regularize or downsize to find the best generalization. Starting with regularization risks never reaching sufficient capacity.
questions.explanation: The page states this order explicitly; chapter 6 (p.206-207) develops it.

questions.question: What is validation-set overfitting and what protects you from it?
questions.answer: Hyperparameters becoming overspecialized to the validation set through repeated tuning; a separate test set, used only for final evaluation, protects you.
questions.explanation: Stated at the end of step 6 on the page.

questions.question: According to Table 20.1, which architecture is listed for generating images from text and images?
questions.answer: VAE, Diffusion Model
questions.explanation: The last row of the table maps Text, Images → Images to VAE, Diffusion Model. ConvNet is listed for images → class/regression, RNN/Transformer for timeseries, and Dense networks for vector data.

questions.question: What does the page mean when it says an architecture encodes 'a hypothesis space'? Give an example.
questions.answer: The architecture restricts which functions the model can represent, building in assumptions about the data's structure; training then searches only within that space. Example: convolutions assume local patterns that are useful at any position (translation invariance), which suits images.
questions.explanation: Whether a model works depends on the match between those assumptions and the data's actual structure.

questions.question: Name three deployment targets mentioned in step 7 and what you should keep doing after deployment.
questions.answer: A web API, a JavaScript or C++ application, an embedded device; keep monitoring performance on real-world data and use the findings to refine the next iteration.
questions.explanation: Taken from the deployment bullet.

questions.question: Cover Table 20.1 and try to reproduce its six rows (input, output, model). Which ones did you miss?
questions.answer: Vector→Dense; Timeseries→RNN/Transformer; Images→ConvNet; Text→Transformer (class/regression outputs); Text,Images→Text: Transformer; Text,Images→Images: VAE/Diffusion Model.
questions.explanation: Active recall of the table is a quick check of your grasp of the architecture chapters.

questions.question: Your labels are integers from 0 to 9, each sample has exactly one class. Which last layer and loss does the page prescribe?
questions.answer: Dense(10, activation="softmax") with sparse_categorical_crossentropy
questions.explanation: Single-label → softmax over num_classes; integer targets → sparse version. Sigmoid + BCE is the multilabel recipe; Dense(1, sigmoid) is binary; categorical_crossentropy expects one-hot targets, not integers.

questions.question: A document can be tagged with any subset of 20 topics. Which configuration fits?
questions.answer: Dense(20, activation="sigmoid"), binary_crossentropy, k-hot targets
questions.explanation: This is the multilabel recipe on the page. Softmax forces topics to compete; a single sigmoid unit answers only one yes/no question; mse with no activation is the regression recipe (p.626).

questions.question: Why does the page say Dense layers are unlike 2D convolution layers?
questions.answer: A Dense layer connects every input to every unit, so it can map relationships between any two input features and assumes no structure; a 2D convolution only looks at local relationships (nearby pixels).
questions.explanation: This is the architecture-prior idea from p.624 applied to Dense vs Conv2D.

questions.question: A binary classifier outputs $p = 0.8$ for a sample whose target is $y = 0$. What is the binary crossentropy loss? What would it be if $y=1$?
questions.explanation: BCE $= -[y\log p + (1-y)\log(1-p)]$; only the term for the actual target remains.

questions.question: Besides processing attribute vectors, what other role do Dense layers play according to the page?
questions.answer: They form the final classification or regression stage of most networks, e.g. ConvNets (chapter 8) and recurrent networks (chapter 13) typically end with one or two Dense layers.
questions.explanation: Stated in the second paragraph.

questions.question: The page cites 'the Boston Housing Price dataset used in chapter 4'. What dataset does chapter 4 of this edition actually use, and what kind of task is it?
questions.answer: The California Housing Price dataset (section 4.3.1), a regression task predicting house prices from numerical features.
questions.explanation: See p.150; the Boston reference seems to be carried over from the previous edition.

questions.question: Without looking, write the four-line 'head + compile' for binary, single-label, and multilabel classification. Check against the page.
questions.answer: Binary: Dense(1, sigmoid) + binary_crossentropy. Single-label: Dense(num_classes, softmax) + categorical_crossentropy (or sparse_...). Multilabel: Dense(num_classes, sigmoid) + binary_crossentropy.
questions.explanation: These patterns recur throughout the book; recalling them from memory confirms mastery.

questions.question: You want to predict both the latitude and longitude of a photo from image features. Which output layer and loss match the book's regression template?
questions.answer: Dense(2) with mse
questions.explanation: Regression toward a vector uses one unit per value and no activation, with MSE. Sigmoid/softmax with crossentropy are classification heads; Dense(1) would predict only one value.

questions.question: Why does applying the same transformation to every patch make convolution layers data efficient?
questions.answer: Because a pattern learned at one location is automatically recognized at all other locations (translation invariance via weight sharing), so the model does not need training examples of every pattern at every position, and it has far fewer parameters to fit.
questions.explanation: This is the e07 argument, developed in chapter 8 (p.259): the visual world is translation invariant, so a prior that matches it needs fewer samples.

questions.question: Give two reasons the book gives for using pooling layers in a ConvNet.
questions.answer: To keep feature maps at a reasonable size as the number of features grows, and to let subsequent convolution layers see a greater spatial extent of the input.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in e08. Without downsampling, activations would be huge and top layers would still only see small windows of the original image.

questions.question: Which Keras layer would you use to process 3D medical scans (volumes)?
questions.answer: Conv3D
questions.explanation: The page maps dimensionality to layer: Conv1D for sequences, Conv2D for images, Conv3D for volumes. SeparableConv2D is a 2D layer.

questions.question: In the multilabel template, why is the loss binary_crossentropy even though there are num_classes outputs?
questions.answer: Each output unit is an independent binary (present/absent) decision with its own sigmoid, so binary crossentropy is applied per unit and averaged.
questions.explanation: Labels are not mutually exclusive in multilabel problems, so each class is its own Bernoulli variable; categorical crossentropy would assume exactly one correct class.

questions.question: What is the difference between ending a ConvNet with Flatten and ending it with a global pooling layer?
questions.answer: Flatten keeps every spatial position as a separate feature (large vector, many Dense parameters, position-specific); global pooling reduces each channel to one number (vector of length channels), which is compact and position-independent.
questions.explanation: The page names both options for turning feature maps into vectors. The p.627 example and chapter 8 (p.269) use GlobalAveragePooling2D.

questions.question: Without looking, write the four lines that turn a hidden representation x into a compiled regression model with three continuous outputs.
questions.answer: outputs = layers.Dense(3)(x); model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs); model.compile(optimizer="rmsprop", loss="mse") — with no activation on the output layer.
questions.explanation: Compare with the regression code block on this page; the key detail is the missing activation argument.

questions.question: According to the page, why are batch normalization and residual connections added to very deep ConvNets?
options: To reduce the number of parameters
To help gradient information flow smoothly through the network
To make the model translation invariant
questions.answer: To help gradient information flow smoothly through the network
questions.explanation: That is the stated reason in e04. They don't reduce parameters (separable convs do), translation invariance comes from convolution, and they don't downsample.

questions.question: Why does a Transformer need positional encoding when processing a sentence?
questions.answer: Attention treats its inputs as a set: permuting the inputs just permutes the outputs, so without position information the model could not distinguish word orders. Positional encoding injects each token's position.
questions.explanation: e06 says positional encoding lets Transformers account for both global context and word order.

questions.question: What two inputs does the TransformerDecoder use, and what does it predict?
questions.answer: The output of the TransformerEncoder and the target sequence (so far); it predicts what comes next in the target sequence.
questions.explanation: Straight from bullet e09.

questions.question: You need to classify movie reviews as positive or negative with a Transformer. Which components do you need?
options: Only TransformerEncoder (plus pooling and a Dense head)
questions.answer: Only TransformerEncoder (plus pooling and a Dense head)
questions.explanation: For a single sequence, the page says you'd only use the encoder. A decoder is for generating a target sequence; an LSTM is unnecessary.

questions.question: What does GlobalAveragePooling2D output for a (38, 38, 128) feature map?
questions.answer: A vector of length 128: the average of each channel over all 38×38 positions.
questions.explanation: Global pooling collapses the spatial axes, leaving one number per channel.

questions.question: Why does the page say Transformers process long paragraphs more effectively than RNNs?
questions.answer: Attention connects every position to every other in a single step, using global context, whereas an RNN must pass information through its state one timestep at a time, so distant information fades.
questions.explanation: The book contrasts the Transformer's use of global context with RNNs and 1D ConvNets (e06); the mechanism explanation is the standard one from chapter 15.

questions.question: Can you list the three layer types inside a decoder block and say which one connects the decoder to the encoder?
questions.answer: Causal self-attention, cross-attention, feed-forward network; cross-attention connects to the encoder outputs.
questions.explanation: Revisit 15.3.3 (p.470) if unsure.

questions.question: What does decoder_outputs represent in the seq2seq Transformer template?
options: A probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next target token at each position
A single class probability for the whole sequence
The attention weights between source and target
questions.answer: A probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next target token at each position
questions.explanation: Dense(vocab_size, softmax) on the decoder sequence gives per-position next-token distributions (callout: 'Predictions for target sequence one step in the future'). The encoded source is encoder_outputs; a single probability is the classifier head; attention weights are internal.

questions.question: Why does the encoder-only classifier need a GlobalMaxPooling1D layer before the Dense output?
questions.answer: The encoder outputs one vector per token (batch, seq_length, embed_dim); pooling collapses the sequence axis into a single vector per sample so one prediction can be made per sequence.
questions.explanation: Without pooling, Dense would produce a prediction per token.

questions.question: When does the book recommend an RNN over a 1D ConvNet?
questions.answer: When the patterns of interest aren't invariant to temporal translation, e.g. timeseries where the recent past is more important than the distant past.
questions.explanation: A 1D ConvNet treats a pattern identically wherever it occurs; an RNN processes inputs in order and its state naturally emphasizes recent inputs.

questions.question: You stack three LSTM layers before a Dense classifier. Which configuration is correct?
options: return_sequences=True on the first two, default on the last
questions.answer: return_sequences=True on the first two, default on the last
questions.explanation: Each layer before the last must output a full sequence for the next RNN; the last returns only its final output for the Dense head. Other options either break the shape expected by the next LSTM or give per-timestep outputs to the head.

questions.question: How does the book compare GRU and LSTM?
questions.answer: LSTM is more powerful but more expensive; GRU is a simpler, cheaper alternative.
questions.explanation: Stated in e08; both are preferred over SimpleRNN.

questions.question: The single-LSTM template is described as binary classification but uses Dense(num_classes, activation="sigmoid"). What value of num_classes makes it a binary classifier, and what is the head otherwise?
questions.answer: num_classes = 1 gives the binary head (one sigmoid unit). With num_classes > 1 it is the multilabel head (independent sigmoids with binary_crossentropy).
questions.explanation: Compare with the head rules on p.625.

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why the seq2seq model has two inputs at training time but generates text with only the source at inference?
questions.answer: At training time the true target-so-far is fed to the decoder (teacher forcing). At inference the target is built step by step from the model's own predictions, starting from a start token.
questions.explanation: Review 15.3.4 (p.472) if this isn't clear.

questions.question: Which condition does the page attach to the claim that layers can map 'essentially anything to anything'?
options: The model must have at least three layers
Appropriate training data must be available and the mapping must be a continuous geometric transformation of reasonable complexity
The data must be images or text
questions.answer: Appropriate training data must be available and the mapping must be a continuous geometric transformation of reasonable complexity
questions.explanation: Those are the two conditions in e06. The other options are not mentioned.

questions.question: What metaphor does the page use for how deep learning models operate?
questions.answer: Vast, interpolative databases of patterns.
questions.explanation: From e07: their pattern-matching strength is also their core weakness.

questions.question: Why do fixed parameters after training make models struggle with novelty?
questions.answer: With frozen parameters, the model can only retrieve or replicate patterns similar to its training data; there is no mechanism to form new abstractions for an input far from that distribution.
questions.explanation: e08; this motivates test-time adaptation on p.630.

questions.question: Which of the following is the page's example of sensitivity to 'imperceptible perturbations'?
questions.answer: Adversarial examples in vision
questions.explanation: Prompt sensitivity is the example for minor phrasing changes; ARC-AGI illustrates novelty; validation overfitting is unrelated.

questions.question: Why are continuous geometric models 'ill-suited' to learning exact step-by-step algorithms?
questions.answer: Algorithms are discrete and must work exactly for inputs of any size; a continuous model only fits a smooth approximation near its training examples, so it interpolates rather than implementing the procedure and fails to extrapolate.

questions.question: In the stacked LSTM template, what is the output shape of the second LSTM layer for inputs of shape (batch, 100, 8)?
questions.explanation: return_sequences=True keeps the time axis; 32 is the number of units.

questions.question: Can you give one concrete example of your own for each of the three limitations listed on this page?
questions.answer: E.g. novelty: a model fails on a new ARC puzzle; phrasing: an LLM changes its answer when option order changes; algorithms: a network trained on short additions fails on long ones.
questions.explanation: If you struggle, reread 19.1 (p.588–593).

questions.question: According to the page, what is the root of deep learning's fundamental limitations?
options: The paradigm of fitting static, interpolative curves to data
The use of the backpropagation algorithm
The lack of GPUs with enough memory
questions.answer: The paradigm of fitting static, interpolative curves to data
questions.explanation: Stated in e03. More data or hardware is what scaling provides, which the page says does not fix the problem; backpropagation is not singled out.

questions.question: What is test-time adaptation?
questions.answer: Approaches where the model performs search or fine-tuning during inference to adapt to a novel problem.
questions.explanation: e04; chapter 19 (p.606) names test-time training and search methods as its two families.

questions.question: Why is o3's result on ARC-AGI-1 not considered a solution to fluid intelligence by the authors?
questions.answer: Because it came at an extreme computational cost, whereas intelligence is about efficient adaptation; and ARC-AGI-2 remained unsolved, showing the approach still falls short.
questions.explanation: e04 stresses cost and that efficient, human-like adaptation is still open.

questions.question: Which capability does the page associate with program-centric abstraction?
options: Discrete reasoning, planning and causal understanding
questions.answer: Discrete reasoning, planning and causal understanding
questions.explanation: Pattern recognition and intuition are value-centric (e06); perception is assigned to deep learning modules (e08).

questions.question: What role does deep learning play in 'deep-learning guided program search'?
questions.answer: It provides learned intuition about program structure to guide the discrete search through the vast combinatorial space of programs, overcoming the inefficiency of blind search.
questions.explanation: e09, compared to how developers use experience to narrow choices.

questions.question: Name the two kinds of modules the future reusable libraries will contain.
questions.answer: 'Geometric' (deep-learning-based) modules and 'algorithmic' modules.
questions.explanation: From the modular recombination bullet, e10.

questions.question: Could you explain the difference between value-centric and program-centric abstraction with an example from everyday life?
questions.answer: E.g. recognizing a friend's handwriting (value-centric, similarity-based) vs. following a recipe's exact steps for any quantity (program-centric, structure-based).
questions.explanation: Review 19.4.1 (p.609) if unsure.

questions.question: What three ingredients does the final sentence of section 20.3 name for AI that mirrors human-like fluid intelligence?
questions.answer: Continuous pattern recognition, discrete symbolic programs, and on-the-fly adaptation.
questions.explanation: From e03: 'blending continuous pattern recognition together with discrete, symbolic programs and fully embracing the paradigm of on-the-fly adaptation.'

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the best practices the page says Kaggle competitions help you master?
questions.answer: Writing custom GPU kernels
questions.explanation: The page names the first three explicitly (e09); GPU kernel programming is not mentioned.

questions.question: Why do deep learning researchers post papers on arXiv before conference acceptance?
questions.answer: To plant a flag and claim a finding immediately instead of waiting months for acceptance, which matters because the field moves fast and competition is intense.
questions.explanation: Stated in e11.

questions.question: What does the X in arXiv stand for, and how is the name pronounced?
questions.answer: The Greek letter chi; it is pronounced 'archive'.
questions.explanation: From e11.

questions.question: How can repeatedly checking your Kaggle public-leaderboard score lead to validation-set overfitting?
questions.answer: Each decision made using the leaderboard score leaks information about that held-out data into your choices, so you gradually tune to it; the final ranking on private data may then be worse than expected.
questions.explanation: This is the same information-leak mechanism the book described for validation sets in chapter 5 (p.173).

questions.question: Since when does the page say financial resources and research headcount in deep learning have increased exponentially?
questions.explanation: e05: 'With an exponential increase in financial resources and research headcount since 2013'.

questions.question: Pick one Kaggle competition type that matches a chapter of the book you'd like to practice. What would your validation strategy be?
questions.answer: Open-ended; a good answer mirrors the competition's test split (e.g. time-based split for timeseries) and limits leaderboard-driven selection.
questions.explanation: Revisit chapter 6 (p.204) on choosing an evaluation protocol.

questions.question: What two problems make it hard to find important, high-quality papers on arXiv?
questions.answer: The sheer quantity of new papers every day, and the fact that they aren't peer-reviewed.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in e04.

questions.question: Which tool does the page suggest for tracking publications by your favorite authors?
questions.answer: Google Scholar
questions.explanation: e04 names Google Scholar. Kaggle is for competitions, keras.io/examples for code, TensorBoard for training visualization.

questions.question: Where does the page say you'll find dozens of high-quality Keras code examples?
questions.answer: https://keras.io/examples
questions.explanation: Guides are at /guides; the GitHub link is Keras Hub's source; arXiv hosts papers.

questions.question: What is the benefit of open preprint publishing that the page weighs against its downside?
questions.answer: It lets the field move extremely fast, since all new findings are immediately available for everyone to see and build on.
questions.explanation: e03 (the end of the p.631 paragraph).

questions.question: Why do the authors say learning is a lifelong journey, especially in AI?
questions.answer: Because AI has far more unknowns than certainties; most fundamental questions remain unanswered and many haven't been properly asked yet.
questions.explanation: From the final words, e11.

questions.question: Which one fundamental open question from chapters 19–20 would you most like to investigate further, and why?
questions.answer: Open-ended (e.g. efficient test-time adaptation, combining deep learning with program synthesis, robustness to phrasing).
questions.explanation: See p.629–631 for the open problems the authors highlight.
